plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 5.2.9
plan.contextChunk: This figure contains two panels, (a) and (b), illustrating the disk method for computing the volume of a solid of revolution. Panel (a): the 2D xy-plane showing region R bounded above by the curve y = f(x), below by the x-axis, and between x = a and x = b; a rotation arrow at x = b indicates revolution about the x-axis. Panel (b): a 3D perspective of the resulting solid; at a generic position x along the axis, a circular disk cross-section is highlighted in blue with radius f(x) labeled, showing that each cross-section perpendicular to the x-axis is a disk of area pi[f(x)]^2. The figure derives the disk method formula V = integral from a to b of pi[f(x)]^2 dx by identifying the cross-sectional area at each x and integrating along the axis of revolution.

elements: x-axis (axis of revolution) horizontal, running from origin through a and b, with arrowhead
y-axis vertical with arrowhead
tick marks and labels a and b on the x-axis
curve y = f(x) in blue rising from x=a to x=b with an increasing upturn near b
solid of revolution: surface swept by rotating f(x) about the x-axis, drawn as an open wireframe silhouette with elliptical rim rings at x=a and x=b
highlighted blue disk cross-section at generic position x, perpendicular to the x-axis
red center point of the disk on the x-axis with label x
vertical radius line from the x-axis to the disk rim labeled f(x) with a brace
filled translucent light-blue 2D region R under the curve (visible in the 2D panel view)
curved rotation arrow around the x-axis near b (2D panel view)
labels: y = f(x), R, a, b, x, f(x)

interactions.label: Region definition
interactions.teaches: The disk radius at every x equals f(x), so editing the formula or the bounds a and b completely determines — and visibly reshapes — the region R, the cross-section disk, and the solid of revolution

interactions.label: Disk position x
interactions.teaches: Sweeping x from a to b moves the cross-section disk along the axis; the readout of radius f(x) and area π[f(x)]² shows how the cross-sectional area varies, motivating integration of π[f(x)]² from a to b

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Connects the flat region R bounded by y=f(x), the x-axis, x=a and x=b to the 3D solid it sweeps out when revolved about the x-axis — the two panels of the figure as one continuous idea

demo_steps.title: Region R
demo_steps.narration: Start in the 2D view: the light-blue region R under y = √x between a=1 and b=4, with the rotation arrow indicating revolution about the x-axis.

demo_steps.title: Revolved solid
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the 3D view: the region has swept out a horn-shaped solid. The blue disk at x shows one cross-section perpendicular to the axis.

demo_steps.title: Sweep the disk
demo_steps.narration: Drag x from a toward b: the disk slides along the axis and its radius f(x) = √x grows, so the area πx grows linearly — this varying area is what the integral accumulates.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World units: x-axis along +X from 0 to ~6.5, y-axis up +Y to ~3. Default f(x)=sqrt(x), a=1, b=4, so radius ranges 1 to 2 world units. 2D panel: filled translucent region under the curve in light blue #bfe3f2 (opacity ~0.6), curve stroke blue #2a9fd8, axes and labels black. 3D solid: revolve f(x) about the X-axis; render as a smooth surface of revolution in pale grey/white #e8e8e8 with dark silhouette edges, plus elliptical rim rings at x=a and x=b. Highlighted disk at slider x: solid translucent blue disc #5cb4e0 (opacity ~0.55) with darker blue rim, centered on the X-axis, radius f(x). Red sphere (#d93a3a, r≈0.06) at the disk center with label x; thin vertical black line from axis to rim with brace label f(x). Orient the disk plane perpendicular to +X. In the source the solid widens from a small ring at a (left) to a large ring at b (right), with the blue disk drawn about 40% of the way from a to b. Volume formula: V = ∫_a^b π[f(x)]² dx; live readouts should show r = f(x), A = π[f(x)]², and accumulated V.
interactionPlan.notes: Regenerate the curve, filled region mesh, disk, and the LatheGeometry surface of revolution reactively on any equation_input change; clamp invalid parses (f(x)<0, b≤a) with an inline error and keep the last valid state. For the 2D view, switch to a flat orthographic-style front-on camera and show region R, rotation arrow, and panel labels; for 3D, show the lathed surface and hide the region fill. Keep both representations in the scene graph and toggle visibility rather than rebuilding. Add a thin translucent 'swept' trail of the disk between a and the current x to hint at accumulation.

authoredContext:
Let f be continuous and nonnegative on [a, b], and let R be the region that is bounded above by y = f (x), below by the x-axis, and on the sides by the lines x = a and x = b (Figure 5.2.9a). Find the volume of the solid of revolution that is generated by revolving the region R about the x-axis. We can solve this problem by slicing. For this purpose, observe that the cross section
of the solid taken perpendicular to the x-axis at the point x is a circular disk of radius f (x)
(Figure 5.2.9b). The area of this region is
A(x) = π[f (x)]
2
Thus, from (3) the volume of the solid is
V =

a

2 dx (5)
Because the cross sections are disk shaped, the application of this formula is called the
method of disks
